title: Bronchiolitis and Infant Respiratory Distress: Assessment and Admission Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Babies and children under 2 years with suspected bronchiolitis in primary care, the emergency department (ED) and the ward: diagnosis, severity, referral and admission thresholds, supportive care, treatments to avoid, discharge and safety-netting. Uses NICE NG9 and the Saudi Initiative of Bronchiolitis Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention (SIBRO) 2024 prevention consensus.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: NICE NG9 diagnostic features, risk factors, immediate and consider-referral criteria, admission and oxygen thresholds by age, six management steps and safety-net advice added.
Medicine plan stays 'no drug indicated': NICE NG9 lists antibiotics, hypertonic saline, nebulised adrenaline, salbutamol, montelukast, ipratropium and corticosteroids as not to be used.
All thresholds trace to NICE NG9 recommendations opened on 22 Oct 2026.
unverifiedSections: The SIBRO management guidance (2018 and later) could not be opened; only the 2024 prevention consensus abstract was read. Saudi-specific management differences, including any hypertonic saline or high-flow advice, are not included.
Nirsevimab and palivizumab dosing and eligibility from SIBRO 2024 were not available in the opened abstract and are not given.
Normal values for respiratory rate are given as the NICE referral thresholds; age-specific normal ranges are not from the cited source.
Distinguishing features for differentials come from NICE NG9 1.1.6–1.1.7 where stated; others are clinical descriptions.

pathophysiology.summary: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower respiratory tract infection; respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause (SIBRO 2024, Abstract). It affects children under 2, most often in the first year, peaking at 3–6 months (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.1). Symptoms peak at days 3–5 and cough resolves in about 90% within 3 weeks (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.2). Young infants under about 6 weeks may present with apnoea alone (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.5).
keyMechanisms: RSV is the leading cause; prevalence 25–88% in Saudi studies (SIBRO 2024, Abstract).
Small-airway inflammation causes tachypnoea, recession, wheeze and crackles (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.3).
Peak at days 3–5; poor feeding often starts after day 3–5 (NICE NG9, Recommendations 1.1.2 and 1.1.4).
Apnoea may be the only sign under 6 weeks (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.5).
No effective antiviral treatment; passive immunisation reduces RSV admissions in high-risk children (SIBRO 2024, Abstract).

symptoms: Coryzal prodrome for 1–3 days (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.3).
Fever in about 30%, usually below 39 °C (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.4).
Poor feeding, typically after 3–5 days (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.4).
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea or chest recession (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.3).
Wheeze or crackles on auscultation (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.3).
Oxygen saturation measured in every suspected case (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.8).
redFlags: Apnoea, observed or reported (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.1).
Child looks seriously unwell (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.1).
Severe distress: grunting, marked recession or respiratory rate over 70/min (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.1).
Exhaustion, recurrent apnoea or failure to keep saturation despite oxygen — impending respiratory failure (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.10).
precipitants: Chronic lung disease, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.3).
Haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.3).
Age under 3 months; birth before 32 weeks (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.3).
Neuromuscular disorders or immunodeficiency (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.3).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever over 39 °C and/or persistently focal crackles (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.6).
Older infant with persistent wheeze without crackles, recurrent episodes or atopy (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.7).

differentials.condition: Congenital heart disease presenting with failure
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Murmur, hepatomegaly or poor perfusion out of proportion to chest signs.
Apnoea or lethargy without coryza or chest signs; follow the infant fever pathway.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Coryzal prodrome 1–3 days, then persistent cough, tachypnoea or recession (or both), and wheeze or crackles (or both), under 2 years (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.3).

Apnoea; saturation persistently below 90% in air at 6 weeks and over, or below 92% under 6 weeks or with an underlying condition; intake 50–75% of usual; persisting severe distress (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.3.2).
Respiratory rate over 60/min; intake 50–75% of usual or dehydration; saturation persistently below 92% in air (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.2).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistently below 90% or 92% by age group
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Measure in every child; sets oxygen, admission and discharge.
ruleIn.normalValue: At or above 90% in air (6 weeks and over); at or above 92% (under 6 weeks or underlying condition)

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and measure saturation
actions: Confirm the clinical picture (see Diagnostic criteria) (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.3).
Measure oxygen saturation in every child (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.1.8).
Check risk factors for severe disease (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer by severity
actions: Immediate (usually by ambulance): apnoea, seriously unwell, severe distress, central cyanosis (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.1).
Consider referral: respiratory rate over 60/min, intake 50–75%, dehydration, saturation persistently below 92% (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.2.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide on admission
actions: Admit for apnoea, low saturation by age band, intake 50–75% or persisting severe distress (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.3.2).
Lower threshold with risk factors (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.3.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care
actions: Oxygen if saturation persistently below 90% (6 weeks and over) or below 92% (under 6 weeks or underlying condition) (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.4.4).
Nasogastric or orogastric fluids if oral intake is not enough; isotonic intravenous fluids if not tolerated or respiratory failure is impending (NICE NG9, Recommendations 1.4.11–1.4.12).
Upper airway suction only for distress or feeding difficulty from secretions, and always for apnoea (NICE NG9, Recommendations 1.4.6–1.4.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate
actions: Consider continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for impending respiratory failure (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.4.5).
Capillary blood gas when distress worsens on over 50% oxygen (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.4.10).
Chest X-ray if intensive care is proposed (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.3.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge and safety-net
actions: Discharge when stable, feeding adequately and saturation above 90% (6 weeks and over) or above 92% (under 6 weeks or underlying condition) for 4 hours including sleep (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.5.1).
Give safety-net advice (see Patient education) (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.6.1).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine treats bronchiolitis. Do not use antibiotics, hypertonic saline, nebulised adrenaline, salbutamol, montelukast, ipratropium bromide, systemic or inhaled corticosteroids, or corticosteroids with nebulised adrenaline (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.4.3). Oxygen is given by the thresholds in Management. RSV immunisation is a prevention pathway (SIBRO 2024).

learningObjectives: Avoid treatments that do not help.
keyPoints: Saturation threshold is 90% from 6 weeks, 92% under 6 weeks or with comorbidity.
No routine bloods, X-ray or blood gas.
Discharge needs 4 hours of adequate saturation including sleep.
pitfalls: Missing apnoea as the only sign in a young infant.
Discharging before a sleep period at target saturation.

patientEducation: Return immediately for grunting, nasal flaring or marked recession (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.6.1).
Return if fluid intake falls to 50–75% of normal or no wet nappy for 12 hours (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.6.1).
Return for apnoea, blue colour or exhaustion (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.6.1).
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid smoking in the home (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.6.1).
mdtReferrals: Paediatric critical care for impending respiratory failure
Physiotherapy only where comorbidities impair secretion clearance (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.4.2)
dischargeCriteria: Saturation in air above 90% (6 weeks and over) or above 92% (under 6 weeks or underlying condition) for 4 hours including sleep (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.5.1).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Give follow-up arrangements and how to get urgent help (NICE NG9, Recommendation 1.6.1); review high-risk infants for RSV immunisation per the Saudi programme (SIBRO 2024).
